item.title: Smithsonian Head Assures Staff of Independence After Glimpse of White House Overhaul Plan
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: In-depth reporting on institutional independence and political influence in the arts, with clear and structured prose.

Outgoing Smithsonian Secretary Lonnie G. Bunch III reasserted the institution’s independence in a letter to his staff after a leaked document from a Trump aide laid out a sweeping overhaul of its programming and personnel.

“The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in the letter, which the New York Times reviewed and first reported. “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.”

The document, titled “Smithsonian Institution Renewal Plan,” was photographed on a laptop that a Trump aide was using on the Washington Metro. As first reported by ProPublica, its 25-item action list includes plans to dismiss top curators and administrators, among them Anthea M. Hartig, director of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, whom the White House has accused of promoting “radical activist ideology.”

The plan also calls for a new permanent exhibit, “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance,” and another on “Great Families of American History.” It envisions a “Colossus Statue” of George Washington at the museum’s entrance, which would fulfill a request Trump made in September.

The plan appears to be a work in progress: Photos show the aide brainstorming additions in a notebook. One handwritten entry seems to read “No X-rated exhibition policy,” an apparent callback to a particularly contentious stretch of Hartig’s testimony, when lawmakers questioned her about images of bondage wear in an LGBTQ history exhibition. On Monday, ProPublica identified the staffer as an associate policy adviser with the Domestic Policy Council, the White House office behind a 162-page report that accused the Smithsonian of “extreme political activism that seeks to transform our country.”

A central complaint of the report was what its authors characterized as anti-white bias at the museum, which they said showed in its promotion of diversity, equity, and inclusion. The report accused one exhibition, “Many Voices, One Nation,” of trying “to convince visitors that illegal aliens are entitled to citizenship, voting rights and ‘belonging’ in America.” (Two weeks after the report’s release, Trump signed an executive order directing that signs be installed outside the museum warning visitors of its “ideological capture.”)

The document glimpsed on the staffer’s laptop laid out new interpretive guidelines for exhibits, including an explicit end to the Smithsonian’s use of a diversity style guide. The Smithsonian’s strategy for traveling exhibitions would be reviewed, and one show now on tour, “The Bias Inside Us,” would be halted. Grants to “woke third parties,” such as the American Alliance of Museums, would also be reviewed.

The Smithsonian’s online K-12 curriculum would be overhauled to “realign educational materials with patriotism, not ideology.” The “Becoming US” module on immigration, for example, would be deleted and replaced with a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage.”

The Smithsonian, a network of 21 museums, is structured to operate independently of the White House. It’s governed by a 17-member Board of Regents: the Chief Justice of the United States, John G. Roberts Jr.; the Vice President, JD Vance; six members of Congress from both parties; and nine private citizens. Legally, the Smithsonian answers to Congress, not the White House, but federal money makes up about 60 percent of its budget. Trump proposed cutting that funding by roughly 12 percent for fiscal year 2026, a threat that ultimately went unrealized.

Bunch, who became secretary in 2019, has repeatedly asserted the institution’s legal independence as pressure from the White House has mounted. The administration has demanded that the Smithsonian turn over internal materials and pushed for the firing of Kim Sajet, the director of the National Portrait Gallery, whom Trump had called “highly partisan.” Sajet ultimately resigned. Bunch has drawn similar attacks: a White House aide reportedly called him a “rabid partisan.”

In a May interview with the New York Times, Bunch seemed to acknowledge that recent vacancies on the Board of Regents had weakened his position, though he still appeared to have the support of a majority of the board. In September, he announced that he would retire at the end of the year.

In his letter to staff on Tuesday, Bunch wrote, “As I have said before, we welcome scrutiny of our work, and even disagreement. The Smithsonian will continue to be driven by scholarship, research and reflection, free from outside influence and in service to the American people.”

item.title: Tate Liverpool Plans Fall 2027 Reopening With Surrealism Survey
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed information on a significant museum reopening with a focus on Surrealism, offering a rich context for learning.

Tate Liverpool will reopen in fall 2027 after a £30 million transformation with the exhibition “Surrealism: Staging Dream Worlds,” a nod to the museum’s inaugural Surrealist show in 1988.

The surrealism exhibition will run from fall 2027 to spring 2028 and include works by Salvador Dalí, Eileen Agar and Man Ray. According to Tate Liverpool, the show will also explore the “important role of surrealism in the history of theater and dance” through the movement’s major commissions for stage sets and costumes. Also on view will be Dorothea Tanning’s costume designs for the ballet The Witch, photographs of Sheila Legge performing as the “Surrealist Phantom of Sex Appeal” at the opening of the 1936 International Surrealist Exhibition in London, and material from the archive of Ted Joans.

“Surrealism invites us to see the world differently and what better way to reopen Tate Liverpool. This exhibition will spark imaginations, surprise visitors and reward curiosity, offering a fresh perspective on one of art’s most celebrated movements. It also brings a wonderful echo of the surrealist exhibition that opened our gallery in 1988, while taking visitors on an exciting new journey,” said Jemima Pyne, interim director of the Tate Liverpool, in a statement.

Tate Liverpool closed in October 2023 and was scheduled to reopen in 2025, but fundraising difficulties pushed the date back to 2027. The architecture firm 6a architects is redesigning the gallery’s home, an 1846 warehouse on the Royal Albert Dock, as part of a £35 million ($46.5 million) renovation.

item.description:

Why it is here: Engaging photography and narrative that provides a deep dive into the cultural significance of a specific horse breed, with useful vocabulary.

Run with the Semi-Wild Yilki Horses of Anatolia in Nur Tucker’s Captivating Photos

Around the dusty plains and otherworldly volcanic rock formations of the historical region of Cappadocia, a millennia-old tradition continues. Here in Central Anatolia, Turkey, horses have been a part of daily life, civic programs, and military campaigns since prehistory. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, photographer Nur Tucker captures a portrait of the region’s living heritage.

Published by Hemeria, the title delves into the beauty and tenacity of the semi-wild horses while also highlighting the lifestyles of those who herd them through rugged landscapes. Tucker, who is a British-Turkish photographer based in the U.K., has long been drawn to the vigor and elegance of horses, and the yilki breed that populates Anatolia have a particularly resonant history.

“Yilki” comes from the Turkish verb yılmak, which means “to flee” or “to be set loose.” The name “has come to describe the condition of these herds that live between liberation and loss, between domestic heritage and wild abandon,” says a statement.

In a place where horses have been bred for agriculture, transportation, battle, and more for thousands of years, their role forever changed within just the past century due to mechanization and industrialization. With motorized tractors, trucks, and cars to work the fields and provide transportation, horses essentially became redundant. Released to fend for themselves, they survived harsh winters, bred on their own, and grew into sizable herds. In The Untold Story of the Yilki Horse, Tucker composes a love letter to these striking animals, celebrating their resilience through more than 100 images.

The book is available for purchase directly from Hemeria, and it’s slated for worldwide release next October. See more on Tucker’s Instagram.

Why it is here: Well-written article about an interactive art installation, with clear descriptions and insights into the artist's intent.

A Sculptural Playground in Shanghai Is Designed for Human-Powered Play

In Shanghai’s Jing’an Sculpture Park, a monumental new installation by Brooklyn’s Wade and Leta has a clear goal: to get people up and moving in the same space. Titled “Catching Feelings,” the interactive artwork doubles as an all-ages playground with the artists’ signature sculptures and geometric forms. A central tower holds a quartet of slides, while other spinning and writhing elements are designed for more unstructured interaction.

“Catching Feelings” is one of 36 projects in the ninth edition of the Jing’an International Sculpture Project, an annual project helmed by the UCCA Center for Contemporary Art. In comparison to the artists’ earlier works, the bold, kinetic playground is decidedly analog, with any movement powered by the people interacting with its components rather than embedded motors or motion generated by the wind.

“We’re interested in the life and activity around our work—the behaviors it causes, the elations it brings,” the artists say in a statement. “We watched the same grandfather return with his granddaughter to play hide and seek; an 84-year-old and his partner used the space as the backdrop for their video recordings; new friends were made on our ground spinners; we even glimpsed a man in a business suit having a go on the slide.”

“Catching Feelings” is presented alongside monumental works by Olafur Eliasson, Marshmallow Laser Feast, and many others on view through December 31. Find more from Wade and Leta on their Instagram.

item.title: Shahzia Sikander Sculpture in St. Louis Generates Protests and Counterprotests
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Article explores the public reaction to a contemporary sculpture, offering a glimpse into the intersection of art and social issues.

Activists against women’s right to choose in relation to their reproductive rights protested a sculpture by Shahzia Sikander in St. Louis this week, calling for the removal of the 18-foot-tall work titled Witness (2023).

As the organization describes itself on its website, “Too many women are unfulfilled, unhappy, and underpaid in their jobs, but afraid to take the leap into the unknown. We designed a program to guide motivated women through a process to start working in exciting careers and get paid what they’re worth.”

First Alert 4 quoted an activist with a group called Students for Life America associating Sikander’s sculpture with the overturning of Roe v. Wade in 2022. “Her skirt spells Hava, which is Eve, the first female rebel, to breathe life,” said Reagan Barklage, who related the work to the late US Supreme Court Justice Ruth Bader Ginsburg. “It’s just, you do not need to kill your children in order to breathe life. That’s actually the exact opposite of what that means.”

She continued: “We’re alarmed that this is what they’re choosing to use to represent our city. We do not stand for these pro-abortion rights. And we’re trying to stand for women and true empowerment.”

A counterprotester thought otherwise. “We’re here because this organization that’s located on this block has every right to display whatever artwork they want on their own property,” said Leslie Zacks, who spoke of the protest in the context of a recently failed amendment that would have reinstated a near-total abortion ban. “The reality of the situation is that the people in Missouri have twice had the opportunity to voice their preferences with regards to the abortion issue and have made it very, very clear with increasing majority where their preferences are.”

Rung for Women issued a statement saying the organization “respects the right of individuals to express their views about art, including those that differ from our own. We recognize that Witness has prompted strong reactions and respect the sincerely held beliefs of those who have expressed concern. We remain proud to host this work by Shahzia Sikander at Rung for Women.”

The same sculpture by Sikander was the subject of heated protest in Texas in 2024, when it was decried by a group that called it “satanic” before it was to go on view at the University of Houston. After an opening and artist talk related to the work were subsequently canceled, Sikander said, “Art should be about discourse and not censorship. Shame on those that silence artists.”

An attempt by ARTnews to reach the artist was not immediately successful.

item.title: Dead Man Is Accused of Stealing Art from Michigan Museums
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Detailed reporting on an art theft case, with clear descriptions and context for the reader.

The FBI is seeking a warrant to search electronic devices belonging to a Grand Rapids man accused of stealing art from two Michigan art museums.

According to a federal affidavit, Mikolai Augustine Stasiulewicz, 27, allegedly stole a color lithograph by artist Ellsworth Kelly, from Western Michigan University’s (WMU) Richmond Center for the Visual Arts on June 23. A worker notified WMU police that the work was missing, and Stasiulewicz, who was caught on surveillance video carrying the framed print, was identified through facial-recognition analysis by Michigan State Police.

Stasiulewicz is also alleged to have stolen a 16th-century Albrecht Dürer print from the Grand Rapids Art Museum (GRAM) on July 2. According to the FBI, he had been seen at the museum on June 17, “in what appeared to be a pre-theft surveillance visit.” Between the two thefts, he is accused of entering nonpublic areas at the Muskegon Museum of Art on June 25; however, Muskegon police said he didn’t take anything.

The FBI, which eventually took over the case, learned during its investigations that Stasiulewicz had met with a man on July 8 at the Gun Lake Casino Resort in Wayland, Michigan. Surveillance video shows him leaving with an unknown amount of cash.

Stasiulewicz was found dead in his home on July 30. According to the Kent County Medical Examiner’s Office, he died of a morphine overdose on July 26. Although the office’s autopsy report rules the death an accident, it also notes that “the decedent is currently under investigation by the FBI for involvement in an art gallery theft,” and that a brother had told police that may have played a part in his death.

Four artworks, including the Kelly, valued at $10,000 and the Dürer, valued at $10,000–$20,000, were found at the home the next day.

On Monday, November 23, the FBI sought a warrant to search Stasiulewicz’s cellphone and laptop computer to determine if any others were involved in the thefts. “In my training and experience, and that of the Art Crime Team, phones and computers like the devices will often be used to communicate with co-conspirators,” FBI Special Agent Evan Alkema wrote in the federal affidavit. “They may contain evidence of communications about what art pieces to steal, negotiations for sale prices, and arrangements to transfer and ‘fence’ the stolen works.”

Since its inception in 2004, the FBI’s Art Crime Team, which handles cases involving the theft, forgery, and trafficking of art and cultural artifacts, has recovered more than 20,000 objects valued at $1 billion.

Stasiulewicz was an amateur artist who studied at the Interlochen Center of the Arts, the FBI said.

item.title: The Critic as Artist (And Vice Versa): A Fireside Chat with Jerry Saltz
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Fireside chat with an art critic, providing insights into the world of art criticism and the artist's perspective.

During Art Week NYC, a citywide festival organized by ARTnews, Artforum, and Art in America, I had the great pleasure of doing a fireside chat with New York magazine senior art critic Jerry Saltz.

Like many of us, Jerry has been skeptical of AI, so I started the conversation by reading him a description of his approach to criticism produced by an AI that was based on a talk he gave a couple years ago. After chewing on that for a few minutes, we went on to speak about how he became a critic, how he became famous on social media, what he thinks about art being produced today, his strong feelings about auctions (he despises them), and what advice he would give creative people.

We also touched on the recent documentary made about Jerry and his wife, the former New York Times chief art critic Roberta Smith. And of course, it wouldn’t be a conversation with Jerry without plenty of engagement with the audience.

Despite its myriad challenges, Jerry still believes in New York City as a center for artists, and as a place with a vital community. You can watch the full talk, which took place on Saturday, November 14 at the PMC Studio in Midtown Manhattan, via the video here.

item.title: London’s New Museum Needs a Better Reason to Exist
item.description:
【AI 精简版】 AI-trimmed version. An LLM deleted boilerplate sentences from the original article and left the rest verbatim. The original link at the end is the only authoritative source.

Why it is here: Analysis of a new museum's design and its impact on the community, with clear prose and useful context.

The new London Museum has been a humongous undertaking: 10 years in the making, costing £437 million in total against a budget of £337 million, and yet, after all that time and money, it’s hard to know where any of it went.

From 1976 to 2022, the city’s museum, then called the Museum of London, occupied a site on London Wall at next to the Barbican complex. It moved to Farringdon, a grittier neighbor of the City’s financial district, because the old building was hard for visitors to find and too small to display the full collection.

The new space is bright and airy, closer to an Erewhon café than a museum lobby. An on-site café, open around the clock from Thursday to Sunday, serves hot chocolate and ginger beer. The furnishings, though, feel random in such a pristine setting: a flock of large plastic sheep meant for sitting on, and shop signs from London fixtures like the Odeon cinema and Morley’s, the fried chicken chain. When was the last time any Londoner saw a sheep in the city? In theory, all of this should appeal to Londoners who have taken up early-morning run clubs, traded pints for matcha lattes and aren’t above a gimmicky bit of decor.

“People are looking for community, and they will have it in the museum,” Sharon Ament, the museum’s director, told ARTnews.

The architects, Asif Khan and Stanton Williams, working with the conservation specialists Julian Harrap Architects, have designed a space that’s inviting.

“It took people until the 21st century to realize that cultural institutions are for everyone, and that’s what we strive to make here,” Khan told ARTnews at the press preview. He wants visitors to dip in and out of the story of London without feeling as if they’re in a museum. “When we look at audiences outside of the regular museum visitors, many find it challenging and don’t feel welcome. This is a welcome for those people,” Khan said. Entry is free, there are three separate entrances, and built-in sofas with reading lights invite passersby to stop in, though few people pass through Farringdon unless they’re waiting for the nightclub Fabric or the cocktail bar Space Talk to open.

Still, London is a city of 9.1 million people and a global center for art, film, music, finance and fashion. Finding stories that capture its quirks shouldn’t be that hard.

The museum is divided into three sections. Real Time, at the main entrance, represents London today and includes Banksy’s Piranhas sentry box. (What could be more London than Banksy?) In the Linbury Hall, Our Time attempts to tie the city together through objects like the Lord Mayor’s State Coach from 1757, the Buckingham Palace switchboard and Syd’s Coffee Stall, an East End food cart that operated from 1919 to 2019. Downstairs is Past Time, perhaps the only part of the museum that feels like a museum. It’s the most educational section, with small rooms on the women’s suffrage movement and the Great Fire of London. The rest of the floor is scattered with a piece of a fatberg, Tom Daley’s diving trunks from the London 2012 Olympics, a chair owned by Charles Dickens, a 2,000-year-old Roman wall painting, Anna Pavlova’s tutu for The Dying Swan and more.

The London Museum is a work in progress and until it figures out what sets it apart from the city’s other museums, it will remain a large crèche, where parents can bring their children to roam freely. But there’s still some hope: in 2028, the museum will open two temporary exhibition spaces, perhaps the museum will finally lean into its London-ness and celebrate the cornerstones that makes the city so glamorous and gritty, from the Teddy Boys of 1950s, Mods and Rockers of the 1960s to the Sloane Rangers of the late 1970s and 1980s.

Until the London Museum gets it right, the city has the Bayeux Tapestry, on view at the British Museum through July 11, 2027, with tickets topping out at £33 ($44). At the preview, word went around that one journalist had skipped it in favor of the 950-year-old cloth. In hindsight, I should have done the same, or stayed home to play Grand Theft Auto VI.
